title: Lecture 16. Logic and Structure of a Preventive Project
summary:
1 What is a project

2 Theoretical model of a project

1. What is a project Each biological species is unique in some way. Humans are distinguished by their ability to imagine complex things, set goals, and forecast. All these skills constitute the most complex activity a person is capable of – designing. Almost everything that surrounds us in everyday life, all the things we use, were created through design. Technical projects, dissertations, diplomas, coursework, business plans are also the result of design. And the further civilization develops, the more the labor market expects the ability to analyze problems and create technical or social projects to solve them, because almost everything else machines are rapidly learning to do for us.

Let's consider the design process with a simple example. Imagine you are sitting in front of a screen watching an interesting movie. You don't want to tear yourself away from it, but suddenly you feel hungry. For a while, you can ignore it, but a moment comes when the contradiction between your interest in the movie and the feeling of hunger becomes too noticeable. The presence of such a contradiction, which requires a change in the situation, the involvement of some external resources, the performance of some actions, is called a problem. Any project begins precisely with the awareness of the problem, the localization of the contradiction, and its detailed description. Next, we assess the situation, determine the most suitable way to solve the problem from many options: you can go to the refrigerator, order pizza, invite friends with food to watch the movie, or go to the store. After that, we provide the chosen solution option with the necessary resources: we perform certain actions, spend some effort, time, and money on their execution (human, temporal, and financial resources). The final stage of any project is the evaluation of the result. In our case, we need to correlate how quickly, without being distracted from the movie for too long, and with what financial costs we managed to satisfy our hunger with food of suitable volume and quality? It can be said that any of our purposeful activities is the result of design, even when we do not realize it. And in simple everyday situations, there is no need for us to think about our actions in terms of design. But when we solve more complex scientific, technical, or social problems, we need to understand the procedures that underlie purposeful activity, following which will allow us to count on the intended result.

A preventive project can be generally described in the form of the following scheme.

1. Problem Modeling ⇒ 2. Model Verification ⇒ 3. Modeling Project Goals and Objectives ⇒ 4. Development and Provision of an Action Plan ⇒ 5. Result Evaluation

2. Theoretical model of a project Problem modeling

In this course, we have already discussed theoretical models, and now is the time to refresh your memory of the 'Research in the Prevention System' lesson, because the development of a theoretical model for a project is no different from the development of a research model.

Briefly, a theoretical model is a mental construct describing a piece of the surrounding world. Problem modeling is a detailed analysis of the contradiction we want to overcome. The model consists of:

  • description of the contradiction (problem),
  • factors that determine the emergence and state of the problem,
  • consequences that result from the problem's existence, i.e., how it manifests,
  • hypotheses – connections between the problem, factors, and consequences. These connections can be directly or indirectly related to the problem and are indicated by arrows, as shown in the figure on the right. Research is necessary to verify the strength of these connections.

Model Verification

The main property of a theoretical model is its validity. In simple terms, this is how well the model describes objective reality, rather than someone's conjectures. Only a valid model has practical value and allows one to expect a certain result. The validity of a theoretical model lies in what it predicts and how well it does so. To answer these two questions, the model must be tested or verified using any suitable research methods discussed in the previous module of the course. Essentially, model verification consists of checking the strength of the connections between the problem, its factors, and its consequences, i.e., the hypotheses. As a result of this procedure, weak hypotheses (and consequently, factors and consequences of the problem) are excluded from the initial model, and strong hypotheses remain.

3. Modeling Goals and Objectives After the model has been verified, one can proceed to formulate goals and objectives.

For this, a procedure is carried out to translate the problem model into an objectives model. This procedure is schematically presented in the figure on the right.

The problem is reformulated into a goal, factors into objectives, and consequences into expected results from our project. It is important to note that while at the modeling stage all factors and consequences that could somehow be related to our problem were considered, at the second stage we only kept significant factors and consequences. At the third stage, the main condition is to limit the project's goals and objectives to the possibilities actually available to us. In other words, goals and objectives are formulated based on the amount of work we can complete within the allotted project time and with available resources. Do not set unattainable goals!

4. Development and Provision of an Action Plan Project objectives become work directions that must be supported by appropriate activities. In project logic, these activities should influence the factors that determine the existence of the problem being solved (this is precisely why we verified the theoretical model).

Activities are formalized into a plan in three stages:

a) Organizational plan – a list of all activities to solve all objectives, which can be presented as a Gantt chart. This takes into account the sequence of activities and identifies activities that can be performed in parallel to optimize project timelines; b) Calendar plan – a list of all activities, broken down into stages with an assessment of their completion deadlines; c) Resource plan – resources required for project implementation: human, technological, technical, material, administrative, organizational, informational, financial. All plan formulations must be sufficiently detailed and specific so that all project participants clearly understand what and when they need to do and what their deadlines are.

5 Effectiveness Evaluation

project The basis for evaluating project outcomes is the upper part of the theoretical model of objectives – "Expected Results". For each of the expected results, corresponding indicators are selected by which one could judge whether these results have been achieved or not. This is often not very easy to do. Not every expected result can have an unambiguous indicator. And not all of them can be easily verified. Sometimes this requires special studies, the cost of which may exceed the cost of the project itself. Nevertheless, project evaluation is a necessary stage of the project, both for justifying project costs and for analyzing errors made in the project.
